segments.en: Keep very still. Up in the trees at the edge of the rainforest, a small green monkey with a black face is watching you, deciding whether you've brought any fruit. On these islands, there may be almost as many monkeys as people.

You're in Saint Kitts and Nevis, two volcanic islands in the eastern Caribbean, separated by a narrow channel of sea just a few kilometres wide. Together they make up the smallest country in the Americas.

Saint Kitts is shaped a little like a cricket bat, or a guitar, depending on who you ask. Its green volcanic peak, Mount Liamuiga, often wears a cap of cloud, and the old crater on top is lined with forest.
Nevis, its round little sister, is almost one single mountain rising from the sea. Hot springs bubble near the shore, and life moves at a gentle, unhurried pace.

The islands were among the first in the Caribbean to be settled by the British, and French and British forces fought over them for years. High on a hill above the sea stands Brimstone Hill Fortress, a huge stone fort built with the labour of enslaved Africans.

For centuries, sugar cane covered the land, grown and cut by enslaved people whose descendants make up most of the population today. You can still ride the old narrow-gauge sugar railway, now a scenic train that winds along the coast.
Nevis is also the birthplace of Alexander Hamilton, one of the founding figures of the United States, and his childhood town, Charlestown, still has its stone buildings by the harbour.
The capital, Basseterre, has a busy little circus at its centre, with a Victorian clock tower, colourful shops, and market stalls piled with mangoes, breadfruit and sugar apples.
Hungry? The national dish is stewed saltfish served with spicy plantains, seasoned breadfruit and coconut dumplings. It's hearty, flavourful and made to share.

Christmas here is the season of Sugar Mas, the national carnival. Steel pan bands play, masquerade dancers whirl in bright costumes and mirrors, and troupes of moko jumbies stride through the streets on towering stilts.
People are friendly and polite. A cheerful good morning or good afternoon when you enter a shop or pass someone on the road goes a long way, and you'll often get a big smile back.
Thank you for visiting our twin islands. Look across the water to the east, and you'll see Antigua and Barbuda, with its many white beaches, waiting to welcome you next.
